Buildbox (YC S26) finds user-facing agent failures hidden behind successful traces and evals. The most expensive agent failures rarely look like errors. An agent can pass its evals and look healthy in traces while still failing to help users complete important tasks. They ask again, redirect the agent, try a workaround, or give up. Teams usually uncover these patterns after they’ve already affected customers. Buildbox is agent analytics built around user outcomes. We find where important journeys break down, show how often it happens and who it affects, and connect those failures to activation, conversion, and retention. Buildbox then tests better agent behaviors and product experiences, giving teams evidence-backed fixes to review and ship. Founders Mark Nour and Trishala Jain met at UC Berkeley and have been building together for the past three years. Across teams at Netflix, Google, Amazon, and MongoDB, they saw the same pattern: companies had plenty of signals & observability, but finding the issues that actually mattered and turning them into a fix still took a lot of manual detective work. Congrats on the launch, Mark and Trishala! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/g-BEkwhg

Osseus (YC S26) is the intelligent development platform for robotics, bringing CI/CD across the mechanical, electrical, and software stack. The age of robots will not be unlocked by better AI models alone. Robot development still involves slow coordination across tools, teams, suppliers, requirements, and testing. Osseus makes this process agentic, compressing the iteration cycle and driving its avoidable cost to zero. Replace a drive motor and the bracket, wiring, electronics, firmware, requirements, and tests may all need to change. Each team sees its part, but nobody sees the complete impact until integration fails. Osseus connects into the tools a robotics team already uses (CAD, ECAD, GitHub, Jira, docs, test runs) and crafts a live dependency graph of the entire robot. It automatically maps each extracted requirement to the components, decisions, tests, and evidence that verify it. When something changes, Osseus traces the downstream impact, runs the relevant tests and simulations, prepares the hardware and software fixes on reviewable branches, and reruns validation before engineers approve and merge them. The Osseus Marketplace brings nearby component availability and lead times into the same design process. Builders can find compatible parts to buy or rent, compare their engineering tradeoffs, and keep prototypes moving. Teams and individuals can also monetize unused components by listing them. Founders Anish Mariathasan and Ayush Patel are Imperial College London engineering and computer science graduates. Between them, they have conducted robotics research at Imperial, ML research at a Harvard-HKU lab, and built agentic systems at Apple. If you build robots professionally or as a hobbyist, join the waitlist at https://osseus.ai , or email founders@osseus.ai ! Congrats on the launch, Anish and Ayush! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/gp3_Mdin

I recently completed AI Connects, an intensive 10-day workshop hosted at German International University in Berlin (GIU Berlin) in collaboration with GIU and GUC Cairo- fully dedicated to the intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Medicine. What MediSkin does: - Detects & classifies visible injuries/skin lesions using a Vision Transformer (ViT) trained on the HAM10000 dataset - Generates patient-friendly explanations and first-aid guidance using an LLM (Llama 3.3 via Groq) - Sends medication & dressing reminders, with alerts to seek professional care when needed Built with React Native, Expo & TypeScript on the frontend, Express.js & FastAPI on the backend, and PyTorch powering the AI model - MediSkin is meant to support, not replace, professional medical care. publications.description: With Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Edge Computing growing at a rapid pace, we find ourselves on the brink of innovation and intelligence, gazing into a future in which education is not only desired but also welcomed here and now. Edge AI has a wide range of applications in the field of education that could help students in remote villages who do not have access to any internet access educational content and tools stored on their devices. AI power systems could take the aspect of personalized learning to the next level, which would allow the teachers to better understand the interests of the students. Edge Computing and AI are said to be at the forefront of new-age technologies. Where traditional methods fail to cope with the new challenges in the domain of education, such as the diverse learning styles, geographical barriers, and an overflow of knowledge. Edge computing, unlike cloud-based computing, could be the solution that offers a paradigm shift by bringing intelligence and processing power closer to the point of learning, directly to classrooms and student devices that could unleash a torrent of possibilities, making education not just efficient, but exhilarating.

publications.title: Cloud-Based Tracker for Prioritizing Rescue Operations Using IoT-Based Drones with Advanced Thermal-Imaging Using YOLO V3
publications.subtitle: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems ((LNNS,volume 1096))
publications.description: During disasters, such as natural catastrophes the immediate survival of victims is at stake. There have been instances where victims who were genuinely in dire need of assistance were not provided with it when they should have, resulting in their extreme injury or death. This happened because the rescue team was occupied helping other individuals who did not need immediate assistance. By prioritizing victims for rescue, rescue teams can focus on locating and aiding those most vulnerable or in life-threatening situations, increasing the chances of their survival. With a limited number of resources, categorizing individuals based on their condition and need for help, disaster management teams can strategically deploy specialized resources, making the most of available expertise. Our research introduces a drone-based solution that surveils the disaster-stricken region to identify victims and launches a priority tracker that tags them and gives their real-time situation details to the concerned authorities. The systems involved in this process are the Deployment System and the Priority Management System. The Deployment System utilizes a drone equipped with advanced thermal cameras that are continuously rotated in all directions to identify humans. Upon identification, the system initiates a priority tracker launcher that targets and tracks the identified human. The Priority Management System includes a priority tracker with sensors that provides real-time data on tagged individuals. This data allows the rescue personnel to analyze and prioritize rescue efforts using Priority UI which displays the sensor readings of multiple trackers deployed. The priority tracker also has a panic button to increase the individual's priority and ensure a quick response. Overall, the paper demonstrates a new system for rescue operations that emphasizes prioritizing victims, allocating resources effectively, and improving disaster response efficiency.

publications.title: KNN for Exploratory Drug Risk Analysis and Patient Well-Being: Enhanced Healthcare
publications.subtitle: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems ((LNNS,volume 1096))
publications.description: The importance of drug risk analysis is very evident in the ever-evolving landscape of pharmaceuticals and healthcare due to the introduction of innovative technologies. With the development of novel therapies and pharmaceutical innovations at an unprecedented rate, the challenges associated with ensuring the drug’s efficacy and safety have also increased. Promising advancement in drug risk analysis has been achieved with the integration of advanced technologies including machine learning and sophisticated data analytics. Making accurate predictions on the safety concerns of newly developed drugs by scrutinizing vast datasets has been made easy due to these advancements. Our research paper provides a versatile solution to analyse the risks of a particular drug that may have negative effects on individuals based on their individual medical histories and conditions. Using a handcrafted dataset containing health records of each patient’s medical history, we have trained a K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN) model using clustering methods that identify which patients may safely use this medication and who cannot with an accuracy of 84%. This sophisticated solution can help doctors determine the safety of a particular drug without causing any health complications with the existing medical conditions of the patient.

publications.title: Advancing Road Safety: Deep Learning-Powered Real-Time Driver State Assessment and R-CNN for Proximity Vehicle Monitoring
publications.subtitle: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems ((LNNS,volume 1086)): Doctoral Symposium on Computational Intelligence
publications.description: In today’s day and age, road accidents attributed to drowsy driving and reckless overtaking are escalating for various reasons. This research paper introduces a comprehensive and dynamic real-time driver safety system that harnesses advanced deep learning algorithms and sensor-based technology. The research is divided into three systems that act as a guardian, meant to detect any such drowsiness, or angry behaviour of the driver and makes sure both the driver and the vehicles behind are made aware of the situation, thereby mitigating potential accidents. Such a system requires continuous monitoring of driver behaviour, taking into account metrics like eye aspect ratio (EAR) and lip distance analysis. The research delves into overtaking detection, which is done by integrating ultrasonic sensors, the Collision Prediction System measures the proximity between the vehicle and the other vehicles ahead of it and alerts the driver and honks when the distance is at very close proximity. Our system uses a camera to monitor the driver’s facial expression and issues warnings through the rear alert display and interior lighting cues if drowsiness or anger is detected. If extreme drowsiness is detected, immediate intervention is triggered through visual and auditory cues. The Overtake Safety Awareness System makes use of the front cameras and gives a view of the subject vehicle to the rear vehicles. Experimentation of the system showcases an overtaking vehicle detection accuracy exceeding 90%, signifying its robustness in identifying critical driving scenarios. Through its innovative blend of advanced sensors, intelligent algorithms and driver-centric design this research paper talks about the implementation of a real-time driver safety system that adeptly identifies and prevents drowsy driving and reckless overtaking.

publications.title: Cloud-Based Real-Time Sign Language Detection and Voice Synthesis for Impaired Individuals Using Machine Learning
publications.subtitle: Cognitive Computing and Information Processing (CCIP 2023)
publications.description: Individuals with hearing and speech impairments find it harder to communicate in real time as they can primarily speak sign language and the general public usually requires a translator for them to understand. Therefore, there is a requirement for a system that translates the sign language gestures into audible speech in real-time, ensuring them an opportunity to communicate. This research paper presents a cloud-based solution that offers real-time sign language recognition and text-to-speech conversion websites leveraging a Random Forest classifier. The user can turn on their webcam to detect sign language in real-time and display each letter recognized from hand landmarks detected by the cloud-deployed Random Forest model and store it in a text file. Once the recording of the video is done, the user is immediately provided with an audio file of the converted text file, through an on-screen MP3 player, that is natural and audible enough for enabling smooth communication. Through extensive testing and experimentation, the Random Forest model was found to have an accuracy of 88.2% on testing data and made quite accurate predictions. In conclusion, the paper demonstrates an intuitive and reliable tool for effective communication for impaired individuals, by aiming to empower them with the means to participate fully in the digital age.

publications.title: IoT-based Autonomous Search and Rescue Drone for Precision Firefighting and Disaster Management
publications.subtitle: International Journal of Advanced Computer Science and Applications(IJACSA)
publications.description: Disaster management is a line of work that deals with the lives of people, such work requires utmost precision, accuracy, and tough decision-making under critical situations. Our research aims to utilize IoT-based autonomous drones to provide detailed situational awareness and assessment of these dangerous areas to rescue personnel, firefighters, and police officers. The research involves the integration of four systems with our drone, each capable of tackling situations the drone can be in. As the recognition of civilians and protecting them is a key aspect of disaster management, our first system (i.e., Enhanced Human Identification System) to detect trapped victims and provide rescue personnel the identity of the human located. Moreover, it also leverages an Enhanced Deep Super-Resolution Network (EDSR) x4-based Upscaling technology to improve the image of human located. The second system is the Fire Extinguishing System which is equipped with an inbuilt fire extinguisher and a webcam to detect and put off fire at disaster sites to ensure the safety of both trapped civilians and rescue personnels. The third system (i.e., Active Obstacle Avoidance system) ensures the safety of the drone as well as any civilians the drone encounters by detecting any obstacle surrounding its pre-defined path and preventing the drone from any collision with an obstacle. The final system (i.e., Air Quality and Temperature Monitoring system) provides situational awareness to the rescue personnel. To accurately analyze the area and its safety levels, inform the rescue force on whether to take precautions such as wearing a fire proximity suit in case of high temperature or trying a different approach to manage the disaster. With these integrated systems, Autonomous surveillance drones with such capabilities will improve the equation of autonomous SAR operations to a great extent as every aspect of our approach considers both the rescuer and victims in a region of disaster.

publications.title: Android application for food label recognition to ensure safe food consumption based on user allergen information leveraging OCR
publications.subtitle: 2023 14th International Conference on Computing Communication and Networking Technologies (ICCCNT)
publications.description: The increase in the prevalence of food allergies is a concerning issue in today’s world. According to some estimates, 3 percent of Indians may already have food allergies, the majority under 40 years of age. Food allergies cause roughly 30,000 emergency treatments and 100 to 200 deaths per year in the nation. Additionally, there is a lack of awareness and understanding of food allergies in India, which can lead to delayed diagnosis and treatment. This brings in a need for technology-based solutions to help individuals who have food allergies to identify allergens in their food and to make conscious and informed decisions in their day-to-day consumption of food. This research paper presents an application that helps people with food allergies and intolerances identify potential allergens in packaged foods. The scope of the project involves the integration of multiple technologies wherein the app utilizes optical character recognition (OCR) from the Firebase API to extract the name of the food from a picture taken by the user, and then cross-references the name with a dataset of allergen information. The application provides a user-friendly interface that is easy to navigate and provides clear alerts, Our application is specifically designed to ensure that the user is thoroughly informed of the contents of their food. This brings a revolutionary aspect to dietary consumption by allowing users to have the freedom of consuming their food of choice without having to worry about their allergies and other side effects. In conclusion, this paper demonstrates the successful development and implementation of an Android application that can help in improving the lives of millions of people worldwide who suffer from food allergies and intolerances and can be further developed and customized to meet specific user needs.

One thing we kept coming back to while building Autter: The problem isn’t just code review. As a developer, you want to spend your time building. But shipping something today means a lot more than writing the code. Reviewing PRs, writing and running tests, chasing regressions, checking security, figuring out what broke after a release, and then going back to fix it. And all of these things matter. But they shouldn’t constantly pull you away from building the next crazy thing. That’s what we’re trying to change with Autter. 🦦 It sits across the entire journey of a change, from the PR before it merges, through testing and release, to what happens once it’s in production. It catches issues, traces failures back to their source, helps raise the fix, and verifies it before it ships again. The goal is simple: make shipping software feel less like a never-ending cycle of checking, fixing and firefighting, and a little more like a vacation. 🏝️ So developers can spend more of their time doing what they do best: building amazing stuff.

I spent the past few days deep in The OpenROAD Project OpenROADs power grid internals, trying to figure out why a real SRAM macro on an IHP 130nm tapeout wouldn't connect its power pins to the main grid. I tried nine different fixes. Ring topology instead of a stripe. Halo widths from 10um to 90um. Forced via selection. Precise pitch alignment calculated from raw layout coordinates. None of them worked alone. What actually helped was pulling real geometry straight out of the routed database instead of guessing, comparing what worked against what didn't, one shape at a time. Eventually narrowed it down enough that two OpenROAD core maintainers picked it up, and it's now a tracked issue in their repo. Also got real vendor SRAM macros wired into a RISC-V SoC's memory subsystem this week, PicoRV32 plus a systolic array accelerator I built earlier this year. Caught a subtle address-timing bug hiding in the macro's own datasheet before it ever reached synthesis, the kind of bug that would have silently corrupted data on real silicon. Most of what people see from chip design work is the finished GDS layout. This is the part that doesn't show up in that picture: staring at coordinates at 1am trying to understand why two shapes that technically overlap still won't connect.

A public benchmark certified 2,638 AI-generated GPU kernels as correct. I checked them with a stricter test and majority of them are not. Here is how I ended up there, because it started somewhere else entirely. I wrote the first native Blackwell tcgen05 training backward for the gated-linear-recurrence family, including the reverse-state stage that is usually run in Triton. One recurrence, five models: fix the gates and you get linear attention, GLA, Mamba-2/SSD, Kimi Delta Attention, and full gated DeltaNet. A single backward trains all of them. The standard check is an approximate-equality test on a few random inputs at one fixed shape. It is cheap and reproducible, which is why everyone uses it. But a kernel can pass that and still quietly return an ordinary number where the real answer is a NaN, or give a different result on every run, or break the moment the input shape changes. So I wrote twelve adversarial gates instead: NaN and infinity handling, determinism across repeats, behavior at shapes I had not tested, whether the accumulator really stays in fp32. Several of them need no tolerance at all, so there is no threshold to argue about. Then I got curious what would happen if I pointed the same battery at other people's kernels. 62.1% carry a contract violation. 39.5% fail a tolerance-free gate, meaning no choice of threshold can excuse them. Head to head, 1,487 pass KernelBench and fail mine, against 14 going the other way. The disagreement is almost entirely one-directional, which suggests a blind spot in what the standard check probes rather than two checks tuned to different strictness. The obvious objection is that I just built a harsher referee, so I tried to make that falsifiable four ways: a 7/7 positive control on kernels I can independently vouch for, a threshold calibration sweep with clean separation on every gate, 98.5% agreement with KernelBench's own correctness code, and a stratified hand-audit. On the kernel itself, the goal was never to be fastest. It was to get the reverse-state stage running native on the tensor cores at all, general across the family, and verified end to end. Speed is future work. The preprint is on Zenodo and I want it on arXiv, but as a first-time submitter I need an endorsement from an established arXiv author in computer science. If that is you, or if you know someone it might be, I would be grateful for a message or an introduction. Link to the paper in the comments. #MachineLearning #GPUComputing #Research

This is insane...OpenAI open-sourced a Codex plugin for Claude Code 🤯 You can now run Codex inside Claude Code. Code reviews, task delegation, full session handoffs. Two rival agents in one terminal. 100% Open Source. 25,000+ GitHub stars already. Until now the two tools lived in isolation. Claude Code writes the patch, and if you want Codex's opinion, you open another terminal, paste the diff, and explain the whole context again. The plugin adds /codex slash commands directly into your Claude Code session: • codex:review runs a full Codex code review on your current work, same quality as running it in Codex directly • codex:adversarial-review makes Codex actively challenge your implementation, tradeoffs, and hidden assumptions before you open a PR • codex:rescue hands a stuck task to Codex when Claude hits a wall • codex:transfer moves your entire Claude Code session into Codex mid-conversation, context intact Claude can invoke Codex on its own. If it gets stuck during a hard debugging session, it spins up a Codex subagent without you asking. There's also a review gate. Turn it on and Claude cannot finish a task until Codex reviews the change and clears it. A built-in second pair of eyes on every patch. It runs through your local Codex CLI, so your existing ChatGPT subscription covers it. OpenAI shipping an official plugin for a competitor's product tells you where this is heading. Agentic systems introduce a problem that no one has solved (yet). Traditional software follows clearly defined rules. When something breaks, the failure is usually loud and obvious. Tests fail, exceptions get thrown, or an HTTP request returns anything but 200. An AI system can seemingly execute successfully; meanwhile, your agent made the wrong decision, missed part of a task, or did something you never intended. Nothing has to fail for the behavior to be wrong. This is creating a new challenge with observability. Traditional monitoring is good at telling you when software failed. But agents need a different foundation, one that can tell you when the system ran successfully but the execution path was wrong. That’s what we’re building at Lemma (YC F25) . Catch these silent failures before they reach your users.

I was invited to YC Startup School last week, and I hated it. Not the event. The event was one of the best things I've ever been invited to. What I hated came the next morning, when I opened LinkedIn and scrolled the same post over and over. Same few famous people, same photo, same caption about how surreal the room was. That bothers me because it isn't what the room was actually worth. Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, Alexandr Wang, Boris Cherny, list goes on, were all there and worth hearing, but you can watch a talk from anywhere a week later. What you can't get anywhere else is a few thousand people deep in something hard, standing close enough to run into each other. It's a serendipity machine. A machine like that only runs on real inputs. A scripted conversation of "What are you working on, how big is your team, who's backing you" and then the quiet math of whether to keep standing there- thats not real input. The best conversations I had happened at the very end, hours in, when everyone was too tired to keep it up. One person walked me through the part of their system they still hadn't figured out. Another turned into an argument about the economics of intelligence. One had nothing to do with startups at all, and that's the person I've actually kept talking to since. I keep thinking about why the tiredness helped. I don't think exhaustion makes people honest, exactly. I think it just makes the performance too expensive to keep up, and what was underneath had been the more interesting thing the whole time. It's expensive for the listener too. You can feel when someone is talking at their idea of you instead of to you. So what I'm taking home has nothing to do with who was on stage. Next time I'd rather skip that part and start where the good conversations started. Worst case you meet fewer people. Best case you actually meet them.

For most B2B software companies, the live demo is where deals are won, and it is also the biggest bottleneck in the funnel. Demos do not scale: reps are expensive, they may not be available the instant a prospect is curious, and they cannot be in fifty time zones at once. Introducing Demoless, an agentic platform that embeds directly into Sales and GTM teams. Within the platform lives Messi, an AI product specialist who runs live, personalized software demos on your website, 24/7. Built in 24 hours during the Berkeley AI Hackathon, Messi listens through the microphone (speech to text), thinks, and answers out loud with a natural, low-latency voice. The visitor can interrupt mid-sentence, and Messi stops and adjusts, the way a real rep would. Before stating a fact, Messi retrieves the most relevant product documentation through semantic search, so answers are grounded in the company's real docs rather than random guesses. Every session is saved and analyzed into a post-demo packet for an operator dashboard, so the sales team gets structured, evidence-backed insights instead of a raw transcript. After each demo, the agent also reflects on how it went and creates self-improving learning loops to enhance future experiences. The voice architecture is powered by Deepgram , which was combined with WebSocket gateways that manage each conversation. Anthropic 's Claude Haiku was used as the brain and agent orchestrator, as we wanted to take a cost-conscious approach in scaling GTM automations. The browser sessions themselves were powered by Browserbase , with Redis and Redis Stack integrated for agent memory and the storage layer for knowledge bases of the products being demoed. Linked up with Fisher Zhang , Daniel Lin , and Jack Chen Lexin to spin up this agentic system from scratch and make it genuinely useful in real time. Public leaderboards can't tell you which model to trust in your domain. And most static benchmarks are rapidly beaten. Introducing Augur: it maps where a model's knowledge ends and its reasoning breaks, then generates the data to fix it. Augur separates three things ordinary benchmarks blur: - Knowledge: Does the model know the fact? - Tools: Can search resolve a disagreement? - Reasoning: Can it correctly compose multiple known facts? The third is where real agentic workflows often break. An example: Ask a model who each of five CEOs was, and when each departed. It gets all five right. Ask the composite question — how many were still in the role five years later — and it answers 3 where the verified answer is 2. Five right facts, one wrong answer. That’s a reasoning failure, not a knowledge gap. That distinction matters for training. Knowledge failures become fine-tuning data. Reasoning failures become RL tasks. Contested questions are discarded. Augur builds a benchmark for your domain and shows where frontier and open models are—or aren’t—interchangeable. For example, in our Kimi K3 study, more than 75% of its compositional divergences happened even when K3 knew all the underlying facts. What separated it from frontier models was increasingly not what it knew, but how it composed what it already knew. For Poetiq, Augur closes the RSI loop: Map the model boundary → Generate the exact data to move it → Train → Re-measure. The result is a continuously refreshed map of where models break, plus the data needed to make them better. For customers, Augur produces the custom dataset to fix your model, and the dataset you'd use afterward to check that the fix worked. The exact, domain specific, facts, ready for human labeling, for training open models and testing that the training worked. Full post: https://lnkd.in/gVswZ-bW

Born on this day in 1912, Alan Turing *38 is widely recognized for his achievements in the realm of computer sciences and his legacy in LGBTQ communities. He entered Princeton in 1936 following studies at King’s College, Cambridge, and just before the publication of his influential paper, “On Computable Numbers,” in which he envisioned abstract machines (now called Turing machines) that became the basis of modern computers. After earning his Ph.D. in mathematics from Princeton in 1938, Turing returned to England, where during WWII he was central to the successful effort to decode the German Enigma ciphers, a crucial development in the Allied victory. Turing, an openly gay man when homosexual acts were still criminal acts in the United Kingdom, was convicted of “gross indecency." In order to avoid prison, he had to agree to undergo a series of estrogen injections. He died two years later. In 2019, a portrait of Turing by artist Jordan Sokol of Jersey City, NJ was unveiled at Princeton, serving “as a visible expression of Princeton as the welcoming community we are today, even as we continue to strive to become ever more inclusive and diverse in the years ahead." The portrait is located in the Lewis Library atrium. “For those of us in the LGBTQ community, Turing is an enduring icon, and the growing appreciation of his life and his great contributions to the world are a cause for hope and celebration," provost Jennifer Rexford .

Samuel Wright II ‘22's average workday looks a bit like his days as an undergraduate defensive lineman with Princeton Football: workout, practice, film. Instead of preparing for 60 minutes on the gridiron, Wright serves on the pit crew for RFK Racing's No. 60 team, driven by Ryan Preece. As a jackman, he jumps over the wall with a 25-30lb jack to lift the nearly 3,400lb car in 9 seconds or less. An architecture grad from Lawrenceville, GA, Wright carries many of the lessons he learned at Princeton with him on pit row and beyond. "Princeton taught me that being in the right place doesn't always mean being in an easy place … Football taught me to keep showing up, keep doing my job, and keep being accountable to the people beside me regardless of what else was happening around me." Accountability is a major part of his role race day. "You have to perform in a matter of seconds, your mistakes are visible, there's constant 'noise' around you, and there are a lot of people depending on you. Princeton taught me how to operate under pressure without needing everything around me to feel comfortable or in order first." The pressure came on fast considering this career was never on his radar. While working at an architectural firm after graduation, he received a call from a NASCAR recruiter who had seen his football tape. The size and speed of the All-Ivy defensive lineman as well as ability to be a good teammate met the requirements of the job. "Team identity, team culture, team chemistry, they spread among all of us before that season. We had one heart, one mind, and we had the same goal in mind," said Wright of his time on the undefeated 2018 Ivy League championship Princeton Football team. Wright's love of reading has also been an asset to his performance. In fact, he wanted to be a librarian when he was a kid. In between pit stops, when the adrenaline rush is at a high, you can find Wright getting lost in a book. "That way when it's time to perform, I can rely on and trust my instincts that I developed in practice instead of overthinking a moment." A few years ago, I had to relearn how to speak. Today, I talk to enterprise customers in New York for a living. Growing up in South Africa, I always believed my future was in sport. I spent years training full-time with the national team, chasing that dream with everything I had. When I came to Princeton, I kept chasing it, training, racing, and coaching every waking moment of the day. Then, during my sophomore year, I was hit by a car while cycling. It derailed my entire life. I went through speech rehab and had to relearn how to walk, how to concentrate, how to think. The basics most people never have to think twice about. For a while, it looked like I might never row again. It took a full year to come back. When I finally did, we won the East Coast Championships, placed second at Nationals, and traveled to Henley Royal Regatta in the UK, where we placed second again. By graduation, I had three paths: go back to a national team environment, go to grad school, or do something completely uncharted. I chose Rilla . Honestly, I didn't even know what the company was. In one interview, someone was throwing a football around in the background. In another, people were shooting each other with Nerf guns. It wasn't until I got the offer that it hit me: oh wow, this is a real company. So I sat down and thought hard about the environment I wanted, the person I wanted to become, the skills I wanted to train. And the more I dug in, the more I realized how well I aligned with Rilla's culture: competitive, resourced, hundreds of people pulling toward the same goal, trusted to do what's right for the team. It reminded me of the locker room. I told myself, it's just a year. Who doesn't want a year in New York? What I found instead was fulfillment I wasn't expecting to find outside of a boat. The same competitive drive I only ever associated with rowing shows up for me here. I'm building toward a goal surrounded by people who push me. And I am still growing. Because at rilla, the learning never stops. I get to keep the parts of sport I loved most: the team, the culture, the singular focus, the autonomy to go after a goal and own how I get there. One year in, and I'm just getting started. Excited for what's next.

publications.title: The Influence of Financial News Sentiment on Investor Behavior and Market Dynamics: A Machine Learning Approach to Sentiment Classification
publications.subtitle: Zenodo
publications.description: Financial news sentiment influences investor decisions, but most research focuses on market-level outcomes rather than how individual investors with different personalities interpret the same news. We combined a Random Forest sentiment classifier (80.2% accuracy on FinancialPhraseBank) with a multi-agent simulation using FinBERT on 2,263 expert-labeled headlines, producing 226,300 decisions across 100 agents with randomized perception, portfolio memory, and herding dynamics. The clearest result was about neutral headlines: agents agreed on only 89.4% of neutral headlines compared to 98-99% for positive and negative, which mirrors the classifier's 26% neutral error rate. Herding cascades appeared in 32.8% (buy) and 16.0% (sell) of headlines, but ablation tests showed cascades barely changed when the herding mechanism was turned off, meaning agents were independently reaching the same conclusion rather than copying each other. A small shift toward caution appeared but was too small to be meaningful. Overall, neutral sentiment appears to be where both classification and investor agreement break down.

The biggest lesson from NSRI wasn’t just the final ranking; it was the process. We faced multiple setbacks, questioned our assumptions, revised our models, and had moments where our project felt far from where we wanted it to be. What made the difference was learning how to take feedback seriously, iterate quickly, and improve under pressure. Every round of critique helped us sharpen both our research and our presentation, and we came out of the competition much stronger than we entered it. For a first research competition, finishing among the top teams internationally is something I’m incredibly grateful for. More importantly, it gave me a real appreciation for research, engineering, collaboration, and the value of resilience when things don’t go according to plan. activity.title: A 5½-hour round trip felt like a big commitment for one day, but a week later I think it was worth it—not for the reason I expected. Going into AGI Summit , I expected the technical sessions to be what I remembered most. Instead, I kept coming back to the conversations about how AI is changing the way companies build products, make decisions, and create value. One point that Jeremiah Owyang made has stuck with me all week: as coding becomes more commoditized, competitive advantage increasingly comes from knowing what to build—and why. That idea resonated with me because it put into words the intersection of technology and business that I've found myself drawn toward. It also connected with another conversation from the conference. Larry Blyth and Ben Haefele discussed how companies adopting AI increasingly value employees who are curious, experiment with new tools, and know how to use technology to solve problems—even when they aren't in technical roles themselves. Taken together, those conversations reinforced something I've been thinking about for a while: understanding technology is becoming increasingly valuable, but so is understanding how to apply it to real business problems. That's exactly the direction I want to keep growing in. I walked in expecting most conversations to happen while wandering around the conference. In reality, the most valuable ones came from staying after sessions, asking a genuine question, and hearing about someone's experience. Those few minutes ended up being far more valuable than trying to maximize the number of people I met. There were plenty of cool robots and impressive demos (and I watched a robot play soccer! ⚽🤖), but the biggest value for me was leaving with a better understanding of how AI is reshaping products and businesses—and with a lot more curiosity than when I arrived. Thanks to everyone who shared their perspectives throughout the day. I'm looking forward to continuing to learn—and hopefully contribute—at the intersection of AI, product, and business, as this space continues to evolve. #AGISummit #ArtificialIntelligence #AI #ProductManagement #BusinessStrategy #Technology ...more

Four years ago, I committed to Purdue with a pretty clear picture of how I thought college would go. I was a Data Science major, and I fully expected to spend the next four years on that path. Instead, I recently graduated from Purdue University with a B.S. in Business Analytics and Information Management. One of the biggest surprises was changing majors after my sophomore year. What started as a path in Data Science ultimately led me to Business Analytics and Information Management, requiring me to fit an entirely new major into my final two years at Purdue. Looking back, it ended up being one of the best decisions I've ever made. I joined organizations I never expected to be a part of, formed friendships I never could have predicted, explored interests I didn't know I had, and found opportunities that challenged me in ways I never anticipated. Somewhere along the way, Purdue became so much more than a place where I earned a degree. It became a place where I grew, learned, took chances, found my people, and discovered what genuinely excites me. Beyond the classroom, Purdue gave me opportunities to conduct industry-sponsored research, work in AI and analytics, take on leadership roles, and be part of communities that made campus feel like home. But what stood out most was the people. Long before I committed, I remember talking to students, alumni, and even complete strangers who were eager to share their experiences and help me make my decision. That sense of community and pride is something I've continued to experience throughout my time here. I'm incredibly grateful to the professors, mentors, teammates, friends, and family members who supported me throughout this journey. Should CS instructors use AI-generated instructional videos in classroom? We wanted to move beyond speculation and understand what students actually think. In our study, 170 computing students across two U.S. universities watched three short AI-generated instructional videos on Markdown created using Knowlify (YC S25) and shared their perceptions. Here are the key findings: • Students rated the videos highly for quality, accuracy, and usability. • Nearly half of the students could not confidently identify that the videos were AI-generated. • Despite these positive perceptions, students were much more cautious about broader adoption. Most still preferred instructor-recorded videos and expressed greater trust in human-presented content. • Students felt AI-generated videos were best suited for simple, supplemental, and highly visual topics, but less appropriate for complex, interactive, or discussion-based content. Our takeaway: AI-generated instructional videos show strong potential to complement computing instruction, but they are not a replacement for the instructor presence and interaction that students value most. A note on transparency: The videos were created using Knowlify, which provided early access to the platform and free credits. Knowlify had no role in the study design, data collection, analysis, or interpretation of the results. 📄 Preprint: https://lnkd.in/ecypCJkd Work done in collaboration with Esse Ciego , Shubbhi Taneja and Wilson Wong, PhD, MBA #ComputingEducation #AIinEducation #GenerativeAI

activity.title: Excited to share our new publication in IOP Science’s Machine Learning: Earth! Over the past year and a half, Cenlin He and I had the privilege of mentoring Yashnil Mohanty , an exceptionally talented and motivated student from Westmont High School (CA). In this work, Yashnil applied machine learning to examine how wildfire impacts the predictability of snow disappearance in Northern California. We found that ML model accuracy decreases in heavily burned areas due to altered relationships between environmental predictors and snow dynamics. This finding highlights the need to integrate observations with modeling to better constrain simulations and account for wildfire impacts, helping maintain snow model accuracy in post-fire environments. Personally, this has been a highly rewarding experience, mentoring a young scientist who combines technical skill with genuine passion for applying machine learning to Earth science. Congratulations to Yashnil on this lead-author publication 👏

The Copperlane (YC W26) team just spent a week under the 100°F Vegas sun to see where the future of mortgage is heading at Mastermind Summit . 🎲 Here's what we're noticing: 1. This industry is more complex than it looks from the outside, and that complexity isn't going away. For any technology to actually be useful to lenders, you have to start from the value it delivers to them. Earning a place in someone's workflow is harder than building the tech itself. 2. The devil is in the details. Many tech tools make big promises and can deliver on typical clean files. The real challenge is being able to handle the complexity of messier files, because that's where most of the real work and cost actually sit. 3. Trust is the real adoption barrier, and in such a regulated industry, lenders don't want a black box. They want to see why a decision was made and have an audit trail behind it. Explainability and transparency are key. Conversations like these shape what we're building at Copperlane. Our AI LOA Penny is designed to handle the incomplete and complex files. We've built Penny with safety first, and she's designed to show her full reasoning so lenders can trust what she's doing. Check it out: https://www.usebanyan.com/ Over the past few months, our team found ourselves juggling: • Prompt definitions scattered across YAML files, docs, and Slack threads • No reliable version history or visibility into changes • No way to A/B test prompt updates without redeploying everything So we built Banyan to bring order: • Composer — drag‑&‑drop prompt workflows with git-style version control • Experiments — design A/B tests and monitor statistically‑significant results • AI evaluation — automatically score prompt outputs and suggest improvements • Quick integration — CLI, Python SDK and Rest API compatible with OpenAI, Anthropic, Llama and all your favourite tools Today we’re opening the free beta to developers and teams building with LLMs — no strings attached, just feedback welcomed. Why this matters: LLM-powered apps deserve the same developer-grade tools as code—clear history, easy collaboration, repeatable tests, and exemplar results.
